name: Karkadeswarar Temple, Tirunthudevankudi
deity: Shiva as Karkadeswarar, with the goddess Arumarundhu Nayaki (Apoorvanayaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar (7th century); brick temple later rebuilt in stone in the Chola period
dynasty: Chola (stone rebuilding in the medieval period)
summary: Tirunthudevankudi, known today as Nandankoil, is the Tevaram shrine of Karkadeswarar, the Lord who opened a hole in his linga to shelter a crab, and of Arumarundhu Nayaki, the goddess of the rare medicine.

sections.history: Tirunthudevankudi, today the village of Nandankoil a few kilometres from Kumbakonam, is one of the Tevaram shrines of Chola Nadu north of the Kaveri. Tirugnanasambandar sang of the Lord here, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and temple lists count it among the shrines on the northern bank of the river. Older names of the place include Karkateeswaram and Nandankoil. The original brick shrine was later rebuilt in stone in the Chola period, though the sources do not name its builders. The name Tirunthudevankudi is read as the place where the Devan, Indra, was set right, a story of a hasty king of the gods and a patient devotee that is remembered in the very name of the village.
sections.architecture: The temple stands in a quiet village setting, and a water-filled moat is said to run along its walls on three sides, leaving the east open. The original brick structure was later strengthened and rebuilt in stone. The sanctum holds the linga of Karkadeswarar, and on it devotees are shown the opening made for the crab and the mark of Indra's sword. The goddess Arumarundhu Nayaki, also called Apoorvanayaki, has her own shrine, and the festival image is Somaskandar. A figure of Yoga Chandra is also worshipped here, which ties the shrine to the Moon and to the sign of Karkataka, the crab. The temple tank is called the Karkata Theertham.
sections.legends: The defining legend is the crab's. A gandharva once mocked the sage Durvasa, who was absorbed in worship, and the sage cursed him to be born as a crab. Told to atone by worshipping Shiva here, the crab brought a lotus from the temple tank to the linga each day. Indra, who came with a thousand and eight lotuses for his own worship, found one missing, and on seeing the little crab climbing to the linga with a flower he struck at it with his sword. The Lord opened a hole in the linga so that the crab could slip inside to safety; the gandharva was freed from his curse, and Indra, corrected, was forgiven. Another telling makes the crab the goddess herself in disguise. A further tradition remembers the Lord as Oushadeeswarar, who took the form of an old man to cure a Chola king of a grievous illness, which is why the goddess is honoured as Arumarundhu Nayaki, the lady of the rare medicine.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri (February to March) and Tirukarthikai (November to December) are the principal festivals named for the temple, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. The shrine is especially sought by those born under the Ashlesha star (Aayilyam) in Karkataka rasi, the sign of the crab, and by those seeking relief from the Moon's influence. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Nandankoil is a quiet village, and the temple, ringed by water on three sides, has the feeling of a place set apart. Approach from the open eastern side, and note that pilgrims often bathe at the Karkata Theertham, where the crab is said to have gathered its lotuses, before darshan. Come to the sanctum of Karkadeswarar, look for the opening on the linga that devotees are shown, then turn to the goddess Arumarundhu Nayaki, whose name means the rare medicine and who is a favourite of those praying for health. The shrine of Yoga Chandra is worth a pause, especially for those born under Ashlesha.

visit.timings: Reported hours differ between sources, broadly a morning session and an evening session (for example about 9:00 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. and 4:00 to 7:00 p.m.); confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Nandankoil (Tirunthudevankudi) lies roughly 7 to 10 km from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, near Thiruvidaimarudur and Thiruvisanallur; sources differ on the exact distance. Kumbakonam is the nearest main railway station and bus hub, and autos or taxis make the short onward run. The nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli, about 100 km away.
